title: karma: the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita
hook: a king meets a young wanderer with nothing, and asks where his calm comes from

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was karma: Uddhava asked to be taken along, and Krishna stayed to teach him instead. Whose way of doing a task did you borrow? Day one thousand two hundred three.

A king out in the world meets a young man who owns nothing. No house, no plans, no worry on his face. The king is Yadu, an ancestor of Krishna's own clan, and he can't help asking. You're clever and capable, he says, and yet you live like a child, untroubled. People all around are burning with wanting, and you stand there cool, like an elephant standing in a river while the forest burns. Where does your calm come from? Krishna tells this story to Uddhava early in their dialogue. The young wanderer is an avadhuta, a wanderer who lives outside the world's usual rules. His answer: I've had many teachers. And the first one he names is right under your feet.
screen: `A KING MEETS A WANDERER.` → `WHERE DOES YOUR CALM COME FROM?` → `I'VE HAD MANY TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: The first teacher is the earth. Here's what the avadhuta says he learned from it, in paraphrase: a steady person, even when pushed around by other beings, remembers that they too are moved by forces beyond their control, and doesn't step off the path. Look at what the earth puts up with. People dig it, plow it, build on it and walk on it all day. It doesn't shake anyone off. It keeps doing what earth does: holding things up, growing food. This is a karma teaching from an unexpected side. Karma talk often starts with my actions and what comes back to me. The avadhuta turns it around. The other person, the one acting badly, is caught in a web of causes too. Not excused. Understood. Their action is theirs. My steadiness is mine. And notice what the earth doesn't do. It doesn't pretend nothing happened. It doesn't argue. It simply doesn't swerve. The verse isn't asking anyone to be a doormat. It's asking them not to let someone else's bad day rewrite their own path. The avadhuta goes on to name many more teachers after the earth: the wind, the sky, water, fire, the moon, a python, a moth, a honeybee and others, each with its own lesson. Krishna tells the whole story so Uddhava can see the world itself as a classroom. But the list begins at the ground, with the teacher everybody stands on.
screen: `THE EARTH: PUSHED, AND STILL STEADY.` · `OTHERS ARE MOVED BY CAUSES TOO.` · `NOT A DOORMAT: JUST DON'T SWERVE.` · `THE WORLD AS A CLASSROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit like the ground. Settle, and feel what's holding you up: the chair, the floor, the earth under the building. Let your weight go into it. Now bring to mind one person who pushed you lately, a sharp word, a careless move. Don't replay it. Just say to yourself: they were moved by things I can't see. Then come back to the weight, and the ground holding you. If you pray, you can hold that person before the One you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action, and the web of causes behind it. The avadhuta learned from the earth that others are moved by causes too, and not to swerve. Today's word.
Your line: karma, the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita. Today, when someone's action knocks into yours, take one breath and keep to your own path. Day one thousand two hundred three.

howItsDone: The avadhuta's list of teachers in the Bhagavata's eleventh book is a familiar teaching story among Hindus, and tradition identifies the avadhuta with Dattatreya, honored as a teacher of teachers.

fork.setup: you're the avadhuta. people push you around and treat you badly. what did the earth teach you to do?

fork.reveal: the earth's lesson: others are moved by forces beyond their control, so the steady person doesn't swerve. no revenge, no running.

original.note: Sanskrit: a wanderer free of the world's usual rules; the young teacher in Krishna's story.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma means people get what they deserve.
what it means: here, seeing that others act from causes they don't fully control, and not swerving from your own path.
what a scholar hears: Bhagavata Purana 11.7.37, the earth's lesson, first in the avadhuta's list of teachers, told to King Yadu and retold by Krishna to Uddhava.
